title: Walking with modesty
hookLine: one of the two women comes to him walking with modesty (28:25)

lines: A MAN ON THE RUN, AT A WELL.
HE SITS IN THE SHADE AND PRAYS.
cards: Musa is a grown man now, and on the run. He has fled Egypt alone and walked all the way to Madyan. At a well, shepherds are crowding their flocks in to drink.
Standing back, holding their animals away, are two women. He asks what's wrong. They can't water until the shepherds leave, they say, and their father is a very old man.
So Musa waters their flock, then sits in the shade, exhausted, with nothing, and prays. And someone comes walking toward him.

teach.h: I AM NEEDY OF WHATEVER GOOD.
teach.b: His prayer is one line long. Pickthall: "My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me." No plan, no demand.
Pickthall: "Then there came unto him one of the two women, walking shyly." The Arabic says she walked 'ala istihya', upon shyness.

teach.h: HAYA' AND HAYAT: MODESTY AND LIFE.
teach.b: The classical dictionaries put that word under the same root as haya', today's word, and hayat, life; some classical scholars, Ibn al-Qayyim among them, drew the connection: haya' keeps a heart alive.
The verse describes her modesty by the way she walks: not her clothes, which it doesn't mention, but her pace and bearing.
And in the same verse she speaks clearly to a stranger: my father invites you, to pay you for watering for us. Modesty here isn't silence or shrinking.
It's dignified and unhurried, and still says exactly what needs saying. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim calls haya' a branch of faith; another, in Bukhari, says it brings nothing but good.
A companion described the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as shyer than a young woman behind her curtain, so haya' in Islam was never only for women.

This week was full of people who carry themselves well: poets who remember, a king who smiled at an ant, a bird who knew, a queen who thought it through, a cornered caller who was heard, a heart held steady.

teach.h: A WALK, AND A CLEAR VOICE.
teach.b: And today, a woman whose modesty is a walk.

how: Muslims speak of haya' as a quality of character for both men and women, shown in speech, bearing and conduct, and many recite Musa's prayer from 28:24 in times of need.

o: a rule about what women must wear in public
modesty, a dignified shyness that is part of faith
the fear of being punished by God

games.q: walking with modesty — tap the pairs.
p: I am needy of whatever good
modesty and life share a root

s: the verse describes the woman's modesty by her clothing
it describes the way she walks; clothes aren't mentioned.
she speaks clearly and directly to Musa
she tells him her father invites him, to pay him for watering.
in Islam, haya' is only for women
a companion described the Prophet as shyer than a young woman behind her curtain.

games.q: you're one of the two women. a stranger has watered your flock and is sitting in the shade. your father wants to meet him. what do you do?
o: walk to him with modesty, and tell him plainly.
games.why: she came walking shyly and said, my father invites you, to pay you for watering for us: modest and direct at once.

practice: Notice your posture right now, shoulders, jaw, hands, and let them settle.
Picture walking into the next room you'll enter at an even pace, head level, neither performing nor shrinking, and saying what you need simply, then stopping.
If you pray, you can repeat Musa's words from the shade: my Lord, I need whatever good You send me.

wordCard.voice: Haya'. Modesty, shyness, a sense of dignity before God and people; in the hadith, a branch of faith that brings nothing but good. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: haya', modesty, from the same root as hayat, life.

carryVoice: Your line: modesty is a walk. Dignity can be quiet and still speak clearly. That's the week, done.
